utterances.text: No, we could not -- I cannot remember that we had any unusual activity in the Famos factory area. There was always small-arms firing from that area, so there was nothing unusual that we had noticed before the bomb explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you refer to this usual -- small fire-arm activities, do you recall that there were -- there were outgoing fire from the center of Hrasnica in the direction of the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, I cannot remember any activities going that way. We always had to take care where we moved when we were close to Famos factory area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in that order here, General Milosevic orders the launching of an air-bomb in Hrasnica and requests the selection of the most profitable target where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted. Major, from what you saw on the ground, was this order acted upon?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't know if I understand you right, but I didn't -- as I say, there was no unusual activities in the area before that morning --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I was referring --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: -- that we noticed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. But I was referring to General Milosevic's order, where he basically proposes to launch an air-bomb on Hrasnica, and that was --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, I did not -- we did not notice anything, as I say, unusual before the bomb came.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour, we can move on, as this document is already a part of the record. And I would like now to turn to another document of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command, and it's already also in evidence. It's P1210. Can it be put to Major Overgard?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I would need the 65 ter number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. 65 ter 10691.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is in front of you now: It is a combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command of the 7th of April, 1995. Major, did you have an opportunity to read this report in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's in e-court. It's actually already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see it, yes. I see it in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And P --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, "the 7th of April, 1995," is the interpretation that I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 7th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we are seeing is the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is document P1201.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But then the 65 ter number should be different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, I meant -- no, it's 65 ter 10691.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] That's what the witness has in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have up-loaded the wrong one. We'll do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made a correction when I mentioned the P number. It's P1782. That should be the document. Is it now in front of everybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it's a combat report, as I said, from the 7th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity to read this report in preparation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when we look at the first paragraph on the first page, we have a bit more details of the fighting on that day, and it says here that at 6.00 in the morning, the enemies, inter alia, opened fierce fire at the Famos factory. Do you have any knowledge about this? Did you hear anything?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No. As I stated, I cannot remember any unusual activities that morning. It was, as I remember it, a quiet, normal morning. Some shooting around, as always, but there wasn't any unusual heavy activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you were in the center of Hrasnica, did you hear any outgoing fire from the center of Hrasnica on that morning?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And one more question. The school in Hrasnica, were you familiar with that school?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I knew where the school building was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was there a military or police unit stationed there?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, that's -- beside the one, there was a police unit, yes, but not in the school. It's on the other side of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if we turn to paragraph 2 of this document, we have responses -- a list of responses, as it is called here. And as the second, we see a reference to a 250-kilogram air-bomb was launched at the center of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Any comment from you on this, Major?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No. It's at the center -- okay, as I say, I did not see anything, but -- or hear anything unusual from our accommodation. We were still in the accommodation when this bomb landed, and there was no unusual activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But what is mentioned here, that is, the response, did you see the result of the response, the response of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, as it is mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- it has to be that bomb which we talked about that landed in our vicinity. I'm not sure if I follow you correctly, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Major. Your Honour, this concludes -- as this is already an exhibit, this concludes the examination-in-chief. And I would now request that the associated exhibits be admitted. They are listed all in the final exhibits table. It's, namely, the photos that have the exhibit number 10466 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And four maps?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- and four maps, right, the numbers 10147 to 10150.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection? They will be admitted and will be given numbers, and the numbers will be circulated to the parties in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Overgard, now you'll be further asked by Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Major Overgard. Let me express my gratitude for giving that interview yesterday to the Defence, and I hope it will help ease the way to elucidating certain issues. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you. There's no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true, Major, that you are not an expert in artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not have any training for artillery weapons and investigations related to them?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I had some training during the course I had in advance of my duty as a UN Military Observer. I was at a three weeks' course in Finland, and we had a crater analysis, we had some technical data and so on. But as I'm infantry, I'm not expert on artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that in your military career, you have never been involved in criminal investigations, in the true sense of that word?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Not in my military career. I have been in investigations during my time in the Balkans, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I meant before that.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, before that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your first investigations were those in Hrasnica; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These were your first investigations; correct?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: These were my first investigation on site. I have been practices during the course -- in my course in Finland and had some documentations on how to do this with me in the mission area. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that in the course of these first investigations in Hrasnica, you were not able to determine the origin of fire or the distance from which the projectile was fired?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I cannot remember that the team did not make the investigations without giving assessments. We were never alone on such investigations. We were at least two or maybe three when we did these investigations, and we always concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, is it true that you were able to express your opinion on the direction from which the projectile came and the trajectory?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, the direction and the general area; not -- never exact placing, but the general area which artillery fire came from and mortar fire came from, we could assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me refresh your memory. Let us look at 65 ter 15890. That is your evidence in the Perisic case, 65 ter 15890. Page 17, the bottom of page 17, and then page 18. If I may, with your permission, I'd like to read what you said at the time. The Perisic transcript, it's page 2959 to 2960: [In English] "Not as I know that there are anything to give exact position, but you can give a direction and from the angle also if you are very good at it, find that distance approximately it's fired from." "Q. Could you tell us on the basis of what you established the distance from which the shell was fired? "A. No, I can't give the exact distance. I only in my reports pointed at directions, and I never had the education to find correct distance. "Q. Was there anyone on your team who was an expert on determining exactly the distance and not just the direction?" [Interpretation] The next page, 18, you reply: [In English] "No." "Q. And when you decided on the direction that you supposed that that was where the projectile had come from, that was just in general terms. You could never establish with any kind of precision where it exactly came from; correct?" Your answer is: "That's correct. If you are not hearing outgoing bang, from that when it lands, you can say from where, but that was very seldom."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this your reply in your evidence in the Perisic case?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you still agree with this answer that you gave?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, it refreshes a bit, and I can agree with and still stand with that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to ask you about the presence of the military and military installations in Hrasnica. Was there a presence of the BH Army in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber something about that presence of the BH Army; their units, their forces, their arsenal?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: There was a headquarter from the 4th Brigade BiH Army, and -- but exactly how many units, how many men present and present at each location, I'm not able to give you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. So it was the 4th Brigade, and sometimes it's called 104th Brigade. Do you remember the name of their commander?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Not at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I remind you that his name was Fikret Prevljak, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It does ring a bell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the headquarters of the 4th Motorised Brigade, were there any other headquarters or commands of battalions and companies?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, there was a headquarter in the area against Ilidza, and there was a headquarter -- I think it was a company headquarter in the -- you could say eastern area from our accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can agree that at least the Command of the 4th Motorised Brigade was in the center, in a populated area; that is to say, in a civilian building? Residential building, I meant.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe any unfinished buildings in the center of Hrasnica, and did you observe that there was a military presence there as well, troops and headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: There were not any, as I remember, unfinished buildings that was -- or buildings that were raised and not finished, as I can recall just now. But I agree there were military headquarters in the area and there were military presence in Hrasnica. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have certain difficulties in noting all that happened, and these difficulties derived from the restrictions imposed on you by this BH Army unit, restrictions of movement and lack of access to certain localities?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It might be possible that -- because we had, especially against the area of Ilidza, we were not allowed to go all the way to the front-line, so what was in these houses, I'm not -- I cannot exactly tell.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see P1782. It was admitted not long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How far was your base, Major, from the confrontation line close to the Famos factory?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Now, 15 years later, it's not easy to remember, but it was, you could say, less than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that outgoing fire can be heard a distance of 100 to 200 metres, outgoing fire from, let's say, a mortar?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, you should be able -- if I understand the question right, you should be able to hear outgoing 200 to 300 metres from a position, yes, normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask you to tell us if you remember these place names: Grlica neighbourhood and Vojkovici settlements? Were these Serbian neighbourhoods on the Serbian side of the line?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I believe they were neighbourhoods, yes. I cannot today say in words where they were. I'd need a map, I think, to mark it and refresh. I'm not refreshed on a map of the area before this event today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Would you please look at the heading, where it says that this document is strictly confidential and that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps Command is reporting to its Main Staff? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this is an internal strictly-confidential document of the Republika Srpska Army?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, it says so in the -- in the heading, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From your military experience, would you agree that such reports should not lie; they have to be accurate, and all the more so because they are not intended for the media?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to another topic. You asked for speculation from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I thought I was allowed to ask leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's not a matter of leading question. It requires speculation on the part of the witness. How can the witness tell whether it's minded to lie or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us look at the incident involving the air-bomb in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your report, the incident happened between 8.00 and 9.00, at 8.40 in the morning; correct?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At what time did you come to the scene?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: We started from our accomodation very soon after the explosion. We just had to put our gear on, and then we went off to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you were there within half an hour?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. How long did you stay on the scene?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I can't say exactly how many minutes, but we were -- I can believe within 15 minutes we were called back by the commander of the BiH forces and told to go to our accommodation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was there when you arrived; members of the army, staff? In other words, who got there --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: There were no staff. We were, I think, the first military on the scene. We just started to walk around to find out what has happened, what is the damage, are there anyone needing help, to have a look. So there was no one when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you explain the fact that the commander of this 4th Motorised Brigade called you back?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: There's nothing to say. That he wanted to do the investigation first or whatever. He told us to go back, and we protested, but we did as he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you of your statement from 1996. 65 ter 10001, page 2. 65 ter 10001, page 2. [No interpretation]: [In English] "I saw some legs and bricks with camouflage trousers and boots." [Interpretation] Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I saw that -- if you refer now to the feet I saw coming out of the pile of bricks, yes. That was the point when the commander came and told us to come to his position, and then he told us to go, to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what happened later? You obeyed, you left the scene, and then you went where?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Went to our accommodation, and then we already found that there was three -- two or three soldiers from BiH Army outside. And we were allowed to enter the accommodation, but were told that we had to stay in the accommodation; not how long or whatever, but we had to stay there until further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to page 3 of this same document, where you say that he did not want to debate anything with you. He turned you back. And then in the next paragraph, you say that you somehow managed to negotiate a permission to come to the scene again around 7.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he was there. But the 7.00 p.m., then we -- I don't remember. But actually I did -- we were there in the afternoon, but we found that we had to take further investigation the next morning. And the next morning, we were also not allowed out of the house, as I remember it now. But this exhibit or this report here, I have not prepared for this hearing today, so I have to review it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope you have before you the third page.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the ERN is 0062 to 0066. In other words, for 12 hours --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- you were unable to move, you were held under guard by the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: We were detained in our accommodation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on that first day, you were not able to carry out any kind of investigation, let alone a serious one?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, not a proper investigation. We just had a look at the scene, and that, I think, was all, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 3 -- in fact, you came the next day: [In English] "By this time the bodies were gone, and the police sent for experts' help from Sarajevo. We only had a short look around the scene, without doing a proper investigation. We also had a meeting that evening with the security officer of the brigade. The first day, we could not find anything, no fragments."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct because --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you have a meeting with the security officer of that brigade, 104th Motorised Brigade, the Muslim brigade?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't remember now. I have not, as I said, reviewed this statement before today's event. So today, I don't remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next day, when you were at the morgue, you were informed that one woman was a victim of that incident?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. That woman we also inspected in the morgue at some point, but I don't remember when. I think it was the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I assist you to refresh your memory. It's your transcript from Perisic, D2977, 65 ter 15890, page 35. It says: [In English] "After that, with the inspector, you meant -- you went to the morgue, where you were shown the corpse of a woman, and you were told that she was a casualty in this incident; right?" [Interpretation] And you said: "Yes." Was that so?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you did not see that woman on the scene, although you were the first to get there?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing her there, that's correct. There were chaos the first time when we were there, so I cannot exactly say that I saw her now, not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we then conclude that all you knew about the scene was what you were told by the police, who conducted their own investigation?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I would not conclude on that, because we saw around us -- and as I've explained, we saw bodies, but to remember the details of that today is a bit difficult. That's the only thing I can say now. I have to review these reports we did and also the questions I answered in 1996, 1997. That's a -- that should maybe have been done before today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at page 3 of this statement from 1996: [In English] "The day after the expert from Sarajevo arrived, in the morning we were first not allowed to leave our house, so we could only go on site after lunch. We conducted the investigation together with the BH police. They showed us fragments of the bomb engine they found on the scene."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you wait until the witness gets the correct page. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on the first day, you did not find anything, I mean, no evidence, although you were the first to arrive there? You arrived before them, and then they showed you the corpse of this woman that you had not seen on the scene, and they showed you traces that you had not found; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we lost the connection. Yes, now we have the connection again. Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, can we say, then, as you say on page 3: [In English] "For the first day, we could not find anything, no fragments"? [Interpretation] Can we, therefore, conclude that you arrived before the commander, that you saw one body --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the legs were in camouflage uniform and boots, and you spent the rest of the day with restricted movement, and it was the next day that you received information and fragments from the Bosnian police?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. And I don't remember what we found on that evening with it, but the next day we found some fragments, as I recall today, some fragments and some engine parts from the rockets. And then we were showed additional parts from the police and the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the fact remains that you had not found anything on the first day; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: As I -- I cannot conclude today without going through notes. I cannot confirm that we found anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at page 3: "By this time ..." And so on and so forth. "... the bodies were gone ..." And so on and so forth: [In English] "For the first day, we could not find anything, no fragments."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I said so, so it has to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that on the next day, most of the traces, including the body wearing a camouflage uniform, had been removed?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: The body was removed. We still the next day found some fragments. Exactly which ones, it's not easy to say today, but we found things and parts from that bomb and rockets. I remember because we had to cut some fence to reach one of them and we had to use our private tools. So we found things on the other day on our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the explanation you received was that you had not seen that soldier, a man in camouflage uniform wearing boots, was because he was not killed, but just wounded, and then he left, ultimately?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That was what we were told, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you find that to be convincing? A man who was under a pile of bricks, where such a big explosion had taken place, was just wounded?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I will not speculate in that. But, of course, I did not really believe it when it was told to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that you hadn't found anything on the scene that would have been of use to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: As I said, we found parts from the bomb and the rockets and -- on the second day. And as I also said, I don't remember, but I think we found things the evening. It was getting dark that evening, but we found things before the darkness came. That is -- just exactly which parts we found, I can't say today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't useful for your investigation, because you didn't know what it was; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I can't remember today if it was useful. I believe it was -- it has to -- everything we found of a device like that, to find out what it was had to be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me refresh your memory. Let us look at the transcript from the Perisic case. 2977 is the page. 65 ter 15890, page 35, from line 4 onwards: [In English] "When you went to --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just wait, just wait. I'm afraid we lost the connection again. Now we have the connection. So, Mr. Karadzic, we have the transcript before us, so could you ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Major, that in lines 9 and 10, you said that you had found fragments, but you didn't know what they were? And the question that reads from 4 to 8 -- well, the question is whether it is correct that these fragments were not helpful for the investigation. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Which page are you referring to now?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] As we don't have e-court, Your Honours, we would need the actual page number of the transcript, which can be found on the upper right-hand-side corner. Otherwise, we're not able to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The page number we have is 2977.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is from lines 4 through 8, and your answer is lines 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just one observation. The witness has already answered now twice the question and said that, of course, each thing is useful. And what Mr. Karadzic puts to the witness is basically a claim from the Defence in that other case. So the witness has answered it now twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very true. So what is your question, Mr. Karadzic? And let's move on from this topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the question was whether it was helpful, whether they found something that helped the investigation, and obviously that was not the case. Let us move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you please focus on your statement of 1996, page 3. The ERN number, if it's of assistance to anyone, is 0062-2066. Can you see that? You concluded that you could not tell from which direction this projectile had come; right? You entered the house, and it was impossible to tell the direction from which it had come? Do you see that? [In English] "We also went inside the house where the bomb had landed." [Interpretation] Do you see that part: "We also went into the house where the bomb had landed"?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] "... direction of the fire. All the windows were broken." Yes, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now ask you whether you remember one of the witnesses telling you something unusual in relation to a parachute in respect of this bomb?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. One of the witnesses from Mount Igman told us something about that there was a parachute coming out of the bomb just before it landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the penultimate paragraph, right? [In English] "A member of the ABH Army." [Interpretation] What do you say to that? Had there been a parachute?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes. That was a witness observation, not our observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you did draw some conclusion on the direction from which it had come, and your conclusion was that the projectile had arrived from the general direction of the separation line; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, from the separation line or the front-line to Ilidza, due to the fact that all the way windows in buildings were broken on both side of the street where it passed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say from which side of the separation line the projectile had come?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I could not say by our own observations that we have to -- and we drew the conclusion due to the witness statement -- the witness statements, or not statements, but what the witness told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the witness who was a member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, and also, I believe, civilians in the area to which we talked to told us. And you could follow the trace, and it had passed over buildings all the way to the confrontation line against Ilidza. So it was our conclusion it had to come from somewhere in Ilidza, from this old farmhouse there in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You investigated another incident, a sniping incident; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, several sniping incidents in the time I was in Hrasnica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before that, let us please have a look at the question put to you by Judge Robinson. Could you please look at transcript page 679 in the Milosevic case, the Milosevic case, 679. The 65 ter number is 10231, or, rather, 321. Sorry. 535 is the page. 55, the page is 55. Judge Robinson is putting a question to you: [In English] "Can I ask you something? Without the statement from the witness, would you have been able to determine the direction from which the bomb came?" [Interpretation] You say: [In English] "We only then could assume, from what I mentioned, this window, that it had come from that direction." [Interpretation] Is that right? Can you see your answer, and is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure where we are on the page. I have page 65 -- 55 here. And what line?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 679. The transcript page is 679. From lines 12 to 14 is the question of Judge Robinson, and from line 15 to line 20 is your answer.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That is correct. I still agree with the answer from then. We could only assume where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to draw your attention to an incident of the 17th of November, 1994, the death of two children. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that that was your first investigation?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since November comes after April, you believe that in April -- actually, sorry, that was 1995. I beg your pardon. Thank you. Do you remember that you had not carried out that investigation on the very same day either?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I know -- I didn't follow the question. About the 17th of November, I only can say that there was an explosion from a mortar or an artillery piece. It was an artillery piece, 120 millimetre, in the children's garden in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, my question was -- I mean, you confirmed that this was the first investigation you had ever carried out in your life. Is it correct that you did not carry out that investigation on the same day when the incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't remember it was the same day or the same afternoon, because this was sometime day-time. If we did that in the afternoon or the next morning, I don't remember just now. The fact is, as I remember it, that there had been people close to the grenade hole and disturbed it a bit, so we could not be accurate on the distance. The direction was -- although traces from the grenade showed the direction, but we could not give any angle to the tail of the bomb. So we could not give any distance on general area from where it came, as I recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems that you remember this well. Do you remember that some children had taken the tail-fin away before you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That was -- that was what I referred to when I said that had been people close to the crater. The crater had been touched, so we could not give the distance or the angle of the grenade, and, therefore, it just was a general direction we could give.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Then you said, in conclusion, that it was most probably the case, et cetera, et cetera, that it had come from the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, we said so. And I don't remember details, of course, 15 years after, but the traces around the crater was not disturbed, so that's why we could give a general direction. But we missed -- or we did not have any angle of the tail, so we could not estimate the distance, as I remember it now. I remember it a bit special with the first investigation we are a part of. I was not alone on the investigation. But this one was the first one, and the result of the explosion was so tragic for a young captain at that time that was still having small babies back home, so that's why I remember it the way I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Okay. The court reporter has some technical difficulty. Has it now been solved? I note the time. It's time to have a break. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00. Then, Mr. Karadzic, you'll have about more than half an hour to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Major, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there, you were given a stabiliser to place in the tunnel in which it had been; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't hear -- I didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What I mean is the stabiliser had been removed, but later on you placed some stabiliser back in place to determine the bearing?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, the stabiliser or the tail of such a device is just giving us the -- from the angle it stands in the ground gives us a possibility to determine the distance. The traces around the crater gives us more the direction, due to how the device is spreading when it explodes and hits the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think the statement should be put to the witness, where he basically speaks about these things. We had it already once on the screen, and he goes into details in that statement, but it should be in front of him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope you have that statement from 1996. It's page 4: "I went on site together with Wilson Ferreire from Brazil the next morning at 7.00 a.m. The stabiliser was already taken by a child, but we could determine the direction of fire by traces on the ground. The direction was very clear ..." And so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that passage?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, the direction was very clear, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, nevertheless, that the police was not securing that site very well if a child was able to carry away the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It can be agreed they had not secured the site good enough, because the so-called tape markings they had done was around -- in the trees around were not covering the crater. So that was not good enough, that's for sure, although all the marks were clear on the ground still, even though a child had been there and removed the tail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Also on page 4, you say that it had most probably come from the territory held by the Republika Srpska Army, and it says: "The VRS lines were 1200 metres away from the place of impact." What is the smallest -- the minimum distance from which a 120-millimetre mortar can be fired?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, as I said, on the data. I don't remember, but it should not be a long distance. So as this was the 120 millimetres, it's -- I cannot -- I cannot say the smallest distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that with a basic charge, that distance is 80 metres, do you agree that between 80 metres and 1200 metres up to the line, the territory was controlled by the BH Army and could also have been the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Well, as I said, in this special case I only can determine the direction. And as the tail had been touched and removed, we could not give exact distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should now like to deal with the investigation into sniping incidents. Do you recall that you were engaged in that kind of activity too?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you carry such investigations on site, taking into account the position of the body on the point of impact, or did you investigate that elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Are you referring to any special sniping that happened or in general? We had a lot of sniping investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to this incident involving the 17-year-old girl. In Milosevic, it was page 637 of the transcript, 65 ter 10321, page 13 -- in fact, 11. You saw a girl heading in a certain direction, and you later learned that she was hit by something?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, she -- we saw that girl back -- or I saw. I then had to go with civilian police to the morgue alone, and I saw that girl again in that morgue. She was shot by something, 14.7 or 14.6-calibre weapon. She's been hit by that one. The wound was through the body on her left side, as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at page 11 of this transcript. It says you first found -- in your version, it's page 635: [In English] "Very first we have to find out how this -- which way was this person facing when he was hit. And after that, we have to investigate the body to see the incoming/outgoing wounds." [Interpretation] Is it true you saw that girl going somewhere, but you did not see which way she was facing at the moment when she was shot?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That is true. We passed that girl when we were on our way from the airport to accommodation, and she was in that direction, you can say, facing against Ilidza. She followed the road and was walking that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 13, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you kindly refer to the real page number so that the witness can follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. It's 637 in the transcript. The previous page was 635.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On 637, you explain that you estimated the direction of fire on the basis of the entry-and-exit wound; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's line 8 -- line 9 is the question, and your answers are 11, 12 and 14: [In English] "An incoming or ingoing wound is a -- more hole, but after the bullet -- when it goes out, it takes pieces ..." [Interpretation] And you say in line 14: [In English] "... and you can clearly see where it comes out." [Interpretation] Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. It might have hit bones, whatever, inside, and then when it comes out, there's a more unshaped mark in the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your common sense or some kind of training that you had to examine a dead body?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: We also had that on the UNMO course, a lot of examples with pictures, a lot of -- or explaining how things can be. We are not forensics, so it's just common sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So there were a lot of limitations, but still conclusion was produced that the projectile originated from the VRS, from the Army of Republika Srpska. That's your 1996 statement, page 5: [In English] "One of the sniping I remember is when I saw a girl ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "From the position she was walking in, the shot had to be fired from the Lukavica side, which was VRS-held territory ." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said page 5?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 1996 statement, ERN 0062 up to 0068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I now ask you, what were your premises for this conclusion? You did not see the person at the time she was shot. You did not conduct an investigation on site, but in the morgue. You just presumed that she continued in the same direction as she was walking when you saw her?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, and from that position she was hit, from there to the front-line again in Lukavica was open area, so we could not observe any weapons in that area. So we assumed, again, and used common sense that the weapon had to be hidden in the hillside on the VRS or Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I draw your attention to the transcript in Perisic, page 2971. That's page 2971 in Perisic. The question is from 13 to 15. Please look at it so I don't have to read it. You say: "Correct ..." [In English] "You just had to assume that she was still walking somewhere and had -- she will not be walking for no reasons because there was firing in the area." [Interpretation] First of all, you are relying on your supposition that she never turned at any point, and if she never turned, the bullet could have come from Serb territory. And the second thing that puzzles me is that there was fighting around. Was she hit by a sniper or was she caught in cross-fire?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: When we passed, there were no -- there was shooting from the Serb-held area behind us, not the other way, even though it could have been, when we left, shooting the other way. So that is not possible for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the Milosevic transcript, page 649, look at lines 3 to 9, 65 ter 10321: [In English] "Later on did you investigate a sniping incident involving this girl? "A. Yes. I was called upon by the civilian policeman to join him to inspect a victim. "Q. And how long after you had seen her walking were you called to investigate this incident? "A. One hour, maximum." [Interpretation] Right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One hour later, you were called to the morgue?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we can only assume that she never changed direction or turned around because of the shooting. We have to rely on that assumption that she continued to walk in the same direction for a whole hour, after you saw her, until she was shot?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, we had to assume that, because people were trying to come to shelter, to houses, due to the fact that there was shooting in the area. So we assumed that, and that's the only thing I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the Perisic transcript, 2971, page 890 -- sorry, page 29 in P890. Do you confirm that you had seen, in the possession of the BH Army, 2.7-millimetre [as interpreted] snipers and that the wound on this girl, both the entry and exit wounds, were large, and that made you think that it was a big calibre?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, it was a 12.7 or 14.6 I assume the hit to be from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered a question by Judge Robinson in the trial of General Milosevic, page 650 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the other numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These are rather large wounds. The entry wound was about 5 centimetres, and the exit wound between 10 and 20 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yeah, it was a big hole. To measure it in centimetres today, it's impossible, but it was -- obviously, it was not a normal small-arms -- small-calibre weapon used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I now ask you to look at the Perisic transcript; page 2970, 65 ter 15890, page 28. And here in the Perisic case, you say that it was --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could counsel repeat the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said "2970."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perisic, page 2970. That leads me to think it was cross-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: In line ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From 18 to 22. And in line 22, you conclude that there was a heavy exchange of fire in that area on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not exactly what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Just a second, Mr. Overgard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's not what is exactly stated here. It's not "exchange of fire," it only says here "some heavy firing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, "heavy firing into the area." Yes. Could you -- I think now, having read that, Mr. Overgard can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was no exchange or cross-firing when we passed. Whatever happened afterwards, I cannot say, but there was shooting from the Serb area when we passed. That's why we speeded up, and we passed a girl, and we came quickly to -- or we had to stop a bit at the end of that flat area before we continued. So what is really the question about it? That was a bigger gun. This was not a small-arm firing or bullet causing the damage on that girl.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Here's what confuses me: You don't say that the Serbs were shooting. You say that there was heavy firing, not heavy weapons. Heavy firing, if I understand correctly, is a lot of firing. This passage from line 18 down --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, there was a lot of fire into that area when we passed, not from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I also have to say that Mr. Karadzic should be fair, because the witness says the very same thing on the next page, where he says the fire came from the east. So it's not that he didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: From the east of airport area. So if you could read through until the first part of the next page, and you will have -- you can clarify further, Mr. Overgard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this previous page, Mr. Overgard, is it true that you accepted it was unusual for the 12.7 machine-gun to be used as a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It was at that time not very often we saw that, but we learned that people also were hit by 12.7 and also bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We can only regret that you did not offer that girl a lift. But what I want to say is that we distinguish between sniping against a person from fire. What I'm trying to say is that you have no evidence this was a sniper bullet.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct. It could have been a result of that firing into that area. It's also what it was investigated, as a person hit, not as a sniping. But she is a civilian hit. Someone has pulled the trigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But it was a civilian moving in an area under fire; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: That's correct, it became under fire. It should not be any firing in the area, but there was, and she, unluckily, was there when it started. As UN personnel, we are not allowed to give lift to anyone, so we are not taxi. That's why we are there, for reporting and investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I'm afraid we may be losing the connection again. Very true. How much longer do you have, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, less than half an hour. 20 minutes, I believe I'll manage to finish within 20 minutes. I'm going to skip certain topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Finish in 15 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should have offered 40. Maybe I would have been given half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, that is not the case. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question from transcript page 629 in the trial of General Milosevic. I'm a bit confused. Line 6, 7 and 8. Is it correct that you sent your reports directly to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Line 6: [In English] "Q. And during time of war, what is the job of an UNMO?" "A. It is to observe, investigate and to report, and we're reporting directly to the Security Council."

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you seen an order of General Milosevic of the 4th of April, that is to say, two days before the order that had been shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope you have it now, D782. Could you please cast a glance at that, D782.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I haven't seen this one before, no, that I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it's from the same commander and that it's being sent to the same subordinate, like the one dated the 6th of April --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: -- the one that refers to --

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Seems so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now ask you to have a look at these localities or toponyms. Actually, look at paragraph 2 and then 3, where the howitzer batteries are, and so on and so forth. Can I now ask you to look at page 2. Page 2, "Tasks." "Prevent the enemy infantry ..." Et cetera. Then it says: "Proskok -- Dujmovici, Proskok, Precko, and Bosko -- Precko, Dejtici [phoen], Ledici ..." Et cetera. Were you aware of these places? They were held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't remember all the names here, I don't at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you: "Prevent enemy breakthrough." Then certain toponyms are referred to yet again. And look at this part of the order: "Neutralise the activity of enemy artillery and mortars." And then: "Immediately upon taking up firing positions, proceed to make fire adjustment with the battery's main artillery pieces and direct fire artillery pieces upon the first detected target." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the order of the 6th, it is stated that the enemy continues to attack within the area of the Famos factory and is trying to enter Grlica and Vojkovici, Serb neighbourhoods? Actually, you know that those are Serb neighbourhoods that are near the Famos factory; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I don't remember just what is said in the earlier documents, but I know the names, and more I can't say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I would be interested in hearing whether you see that this order is sort of a whole with the order that came two days later, that is to say, stopping activities coming from the Muslim zone. Right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Maybe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you whether you knew what the fire-power was of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Hrasnica and right above Hrasnica, from Igman.

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: You are asking about what power they had. I cannot say, because I do not know all of it, whatever was placed in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something now. Is it correct that at Igman, in Hrasnica, Kovacki, Glavogodina -- actually, do you know of Glavogodina, Kovacki, Igmanski Stan -- sorry, Hrasnicki Stan, Malo Polje in Igman? Are these localities where the artillery support of these units was, these units that were in and around Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: The names of the places are familiar. What was there still, I cannot tell you today anymore. It's not what I have been thinking of since then. So we did not -- I only, in the Hrasnica area, once found artillery. That artillery was removed and away when we came back to investigate further, because it was given a protest to our headquarter that was forwarded. So where that artillery or weapons took -- or was -- were brought and so on, I can't tell you, because it was just gone and we never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that Colonel, later General, Fikret Prevljak had a way of making sure you do not see some of the things that he does not want you to see, and that he had ways of preventing you from getting to places where he did not want you? Right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Of course, that's why we had restrictions of movements. We had to negotiate, and he was not giving us access to certain areas certain times. That's the way of doing it. It's a war going on, and they can say one thing, and that's for our own security. Of course, we know, then, it might happen, things that they don't want us to see. That's for sure. It happens on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. During our interview, you confirmed that you spent quite a bit of time at Igman, and that at the time you had no way of knowing of what was going on at Hrasnica, and the other way around; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm used to winter-time or the winter period, especially very much in the Igman area, because I come from far north in the country Norway and I'm used to winter conditions. So I often did day patrols in Mount Igman area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have confirmed to us that you were aware of the fact that the tunnel underneath a runway that went to Butmir and Hrasnica was used for moving BH Army units in and out of town. Do you agree that that had to be done across the Igman road that we discussed and that you actually saw soldiers from Igman arriving in Hrasnica down that road?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, the road from Igman down to Hrasnica was used for, I believe, very much of the supplies to Hrasnica, Sarajevo, and the people coming forth and back. Where, exactly, what routes they used down from the bus stop area, as we called it, up on Igman and down, that was a lot of routes, and I'm not aware of all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You agreed that the Army of Republika Srpska did not show any ambition to take Hrasnica, and that from that point of view, they did not carry out any offensive activities vis-a-vis Hrasnica; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I don't think I agree that there was no thoughts about the taking of Hrasnica. The Hrasnica area I believe they wanted, because of the fact of the localities there could be important for supplies in and out of Sarajevo. So I did not agree with that. Where people walked and where they was transported and how they was transported from Hrasnica into Sarajevo in my time, I am not aware. Just before we left, in that spring, they started to dig that tunnel underneath the airport, but that was not used, I believe, before I left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's time to conclude. I would like you to conclude in two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you agree that when a shell would fall in Hrasnica, you did not call your colleagues from the Serb side, the Lima side, in order to ask the Army of Republika Srpska to stop firing?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, I can't agree to that, because we reported the incoming fire to our headquarter as a sitrep and later on the same day in a daily report, and they did the -- and the headquarter then went to each side to protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. The 104th Brigade had up to 5.000 soldiers, at least three battalions, and their headquarters. You could not see anything except for their Main Staff. Were you aware of the camps for Serb prisoners, Serb detainees, civilians and soldiers, in Hrasnica? There were several of them; near the schools, the basement of the police station, and other places. Did they make it possible for you to see these camps in Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: I did not see any prisoner camps in Hrasnica area when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just the very last question. Do you know that at Hrasnicki Stan, there was an operations group, and at Malo Polje, above Hrasnica, on Igman was the 101st Mountain Brigade, and that Juka Prazina, as it says in this UN report, led a special police battalion, and that the 4th Brigade, all of it, was on those three kilometres that are in Hrasnica, from the line on the east to the line on the west; right?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers in the Hrasnica area. How many, I don't know. Where they were located, I didn't see any camps, although they could be in old buildings around, which was a lot of houses, and we are patrolling, and I do believe that they tried to hide things for us. That's -- that's a fact we know of. I cannot say that I saw any specific camps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major, I thank you most sincerely for the effort you have made in order to testify before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, very briefly; only two points. One is basically the last question or propositions that Dr. Karadzic made.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He spoke about 5.000 soldiers, three battalions, and so on and so forth. Did you see such an amount of soldiers ever in the area where you were patrolling?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No. I can say we saw in the periods and certain days, there were a lot of soldiers, other days less. How many there were, it was impossible for us to count or to make assessments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "a lot," what do you mean by "a lot"?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: You could say when the town -- this small town centre was crowded and so on, it was civilians, a lot of soldiers. It was not possible to count anything, but we assumed that it was soldiers on their way either to Sarajevo or from Sarajevo area, passing through. They did not stay for long anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify one point, and that's: On page 75, line 20, beginning, Dr. Karadzic put to you -- in relation to that girl that you saw walking, he put to you that one would then have to assume that she continued to walk in the same direction for an entire hour. And my question to you is: Do you know when exactly she was shot after you have passed her?

utterances.speaker: THORBJORN OVERGARD
utterances.text: No, that's for sure. And I also wanted to say that it took one hour from, you could say, we were back in our accommodation. When she was hit, I don't know, but then all the messages had gone through to the police, and the police was asking for help, and we did so. That's, of course, not -- she's not been walking for an hour, so -- but I assume, because she was in a hurry probably to come to safety. So it could have happened five seconds after we passed her, so that's impossible to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour, these are my questions, and I was just wondering about an exhibit that Mr. Karadzic, at least according to e-mail, wants to tender in part, whether we should discuss it while the witness is still on-line or not. I don't think it's necessary to have him sitting there while we do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that concludes your evidence, Major Overgard. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for giving it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- despite difficult conditions. I wish you all the best in the new year and good health. Thank you, Major.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and have a pleasant Christmas and happy new year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have those pages admitted, the ones that we marked in that e-mail that the distinguished Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff referred to from the Perisic transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a part of the Perisic transcript. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we, of course, do not have any objection to having the transcript tendered. However, I do not think it's fair to the witness to have only the few pages tendered, as it says here, as mentioned in an e-mail, because it cuts, basically, a certain topic. So my proposal would be not just to have 25 -- 2958 to 2960 tendered, but 2958 to 2963, because that's a topic. In relation to the next topic, the proposal of Dr. Karadzic is 2970, 2971, and to the topic belongs also the page 2972. And in relation to the last topic, which is here in the e-mail going from 2977 to 2981, excluding the page 2979, I think it should be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any reason why not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps. But maybe that should have been dealt with through re-examination. We are interested in what it was that we had tendered, but we don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In order to see the correct context and the correct answer, we need the whole part, so we'll -- just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That part will be admitted as indicated by Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. So could you be kind enough to up-load again, including those parts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a Prosecution document. We don't have the official version of that transcript. However, I believe that the Defence will deal with it with the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That can be done, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will do it accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we give the exhibit number for that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D934. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does this conclude the hearing for this year? Yes, it does. Thank you. We'll rise, and we'll resume next year on 13th of January, that being Thursday. And our new witness order has been circulated. And I wish everybody a very merry, restful holiday season and a very happy new year. And I'd like to take this opportunity to thank all the staff members for their commitment and contribution to the work of the Tribunal. I thank you. We rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of January, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.56 p.m.,
